outputs.final_proof:
\begin{proof}
Consider the coordinate-swapping map
\[
\varphi:A\times B\longrightarrow B\times A,\qquad \varphi(a,b)=(b,a).
\]
It is bijective because its inverse is the coordinate-swapping map
\[
\varphi^{-1}:B\times A\longrightarrow A\times B,\qquad \varphi^{-1}(b,a)=(a,b).
\]
Moreover, for all $(a_1,b_1),(a_2,b_2)\in A\times B$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi\bigl((a_1,b_1)(a_2,b_2)\bigr)
&=\varphi(a_1a_2,b_1b_2)\\
&=(b_1b_2,a_1a_2)\\
&=(b_1,a_1)(b_2,a_2)\\
&=\varphi(a_1,b_1)\varphi(a_2,b_2).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $\varphi$ is a bijective homomorphism, hence an isomorphism. Therefore $A\times B\cong B\times A$.
\end{proof}

\varphi:A\times B\to B\times A,\qquad \varphi(a,b)=(b,a).

The map is bijective, since the map $\psi:B\times A\to A\times B$ defined by $\psi(b,a)=(a,b)$ satisfies $\psi\circ\varphi=\operatorname{id}_{A\times B}$ and $\varphi\circ\psi=\operatorname{id}_{B\times A}$. The group operations on the direct products are coordinatewise. Hence, for arbitrary $(a_1,b_1),(a_2,b_2)\in A\times B$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi\bigl((a_1,b_1)(a_2,b_2)\bigr)
&=\varphi(a_1a_2,b_1b_2)\\
&=(b_1b_2,a_1a_2)\\
&=(b_1,a_1)(b_2,a_2)\\
&=\varphi(a_1,b_1)\varphi(a_2,b_2).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $\varphi$ is a bijective homomorphism and therefore an isomorphism. Consequently, $A\times B\cong B\times A$.
\end{proof}
